I am at work so no access to charts. But just a few quick comments, then later I will post some charts after studying this more.

I have always only considered the top that is getting faked out, and what supply level is getting hit as the old top is getting FO'd. Of course it has to work on the buyers as well. In this situation it seems that as the? FTR got approached there has already been a long drop and sellers are probably becoming exhausted, so they can't be expected to break this demand. So the ITs have to manufacture some more sellers. It looks like maybe a 4h s/r got broken which would prompt retail sellers to adjust their stops lower above the last high. After seeing price bounce off of support and waiting for confirmation retail buys stepped in, then the emotional buyers pushed above the old top for a FO. This prompts the buyers to move up their stops, and the trap has now been laid. The ITs sell hard down to the retail sell stops. The ITs have the sells to break demand without having to do it themselves.

Now this alone raises a few questions in which the answers will be different everytime. Why would the ITs want to break that FTR in the first place? What was that FTR a failure to return to? Was it real demand, HTF support, or HTF R turned S that created the bounce that gave retail buyers confirmation? What kind of supply are we coming from? I believe the answer is in the HTFs, but this concept is brand new to me so now I must study! Thank you!

edit: one more question I thought of: Why would they not want to sell there themselves? Will be interesting to see which way the current flag resolves.

My first attempt at identifying compression. I admit feeling a little uneasy about the way I've gone about marking the chart. Would love to have some feedback.

Hi Miserly_One, the idea with CP is that price retraces to remove supply or demand pockets left behind as it progresses. This allows price to easily slide back to the origin of the CP. In the cable chart today, look how price kept coming back to remove the supply pockets left behind as price dropped. This allowed price to then shoot up to the origin of the CP.

Thanks DrSwing. I guess my gut feeling about my marking was not wrong! I'll find some better examples of CP and post them here soon. As of now, to my simple mind, it looks like that CP is pretty much a case of the base of a RBD reacting off the "base" of an earlier RBD in a downtrend. Likewise, the base of a DBR reacting off the base of a prior DBR in an uptrend. Need to test this for validity.
